1:
Ellicott opens by describing the turn the book takes. The preacher is drawing to a close, he says, and draws lessons unlike those such a view of life has suggested to others: from the uncertainty of results, that we should try varied exertions the more diligently; from the instability of happiness, that we should enjoy freely what life affords, with a chastened joy and an eye to the account we must render. On the first verse he reports the popular explanation, that the figure comes from casting seed on irrigated land such as Egypt before the Nile subsides, and adds the concession that gives him away: it is easier to object to this interpretation than to improve on it. Clarke reaches the same picture by another crop, rice sown on flooded ground and trodden in by cattle, and records that an older Jewish version and the Latin took the words of giving bread to sailors.

The charitable reading is the one most of them take. Delitzsch reports it and assembles the proverbs gathered around it — an Aramaic saying that bread scattered on water and dry land is found again at the end of days, an Arabic one promising repayment, a line in Goethe, and Voltaire's verse advising that benefits be spread magnificently, withheld from nobody however unworthy, and never enquired after. He notes that the Hebrew says on the face of the waters rather than into them, which changes nothing, eastern bread being thin cakes. Henry supplies the farming image, a man sparing bread-corn from his family for the sowing, then a mercantile one: send it a voyage, send it as a venture, as merchants who trade by sea; trust it on the water and it shall not sink. He insists too that it must be one's own bread, since giving what is not ours is injury rather than charity. Gill says the same; Wesley adds the point the verse answers, that such gifts look as lost as seed cast into a river, and that the return, though slow, is sure.

The seven and the eight divide them along that line. Gill takes it numerically — if seven apply, give to each, and if an eighth comes do not send him empty away — while Wesley finds behind it the custom by which a feast's master sent portions to guests and poor; Henry presses quantity too, not a bit or two but a meal. Clarke turns it into prudence: never stop giving while anyone is in distress, since times change and you may need the same help. Ellicott alone refuses the frame. The numbers, he says, are indefinite and the advice is to multiply our own exertions, since we cannot know which will miscarry.

The clouds and the falling tree bring the split open. Delitzsch states flatly that no change of subject occurs here — as it would if the first verse were about beneficence — and that the argument runs on one track to the sixth verse: a man cannot know what disaster is coming, since everything follows fixed laws and the chain of cause and effect lies beyond his will and often his knowledge. Ellicott says it in a line: the world is ruled by laws man cannot suspend. The others read both halves morally. Gill and Wesley make the full clouds a lesson in liberality, Gill noting that they fill as fast as they empty, and Clarke draws an argument for indiscriminate giving, since it is better to relieve a hundred worthless people than pass by one in real need. On the tree all three turn to death. Wesley has it cut us down and fix us in unchangeable happiness or misery; Clarke puts it hardest, that in whatever disposition a man dies he will be found in the world to come, since death refines nothing, purifies nothing, kills no sin and helps to no glory.
4:
The man who watches the wind is agreed to be a caution against a particular kind of prudence. Delitzsch is careful to say which kind: the proverb is not aimed at provident observation guided by experience, but at the useless because impossible calculation of what the weather will do, which puts a man off from day to day and week to week until the season for sowing and reaping has gone. Ellicott states the principle behind it, that demanding certainty of success before acting amounts to not acting. Gill notes the practical outcome, a man who may lose his seedtime and never sow at all. Clarke, who reads the whole chapter as a treatise on almsgiving, turns it against a familiar excuse. If a man is too nice in trying to identify the impostors among those who claim to be in want, the genuine case may die while he investigates; and those very punctilious people who must sift everything to the bottom before they will act seldom do any good and are generally good for nothing, since while they are studying the clouds others have joined hands with God and kept a poor man alive.

The next verse's ignorance is textually undecided. Ellicott points out that the wording leaves it open whether two examples are given or only one — whether we know neither the way of the wind nor how the bones grow, or whether, keeping the rendering spirit, the whole verse is about the child in the womb; he adds that the word for a pregnant woman occurs in that sense nowhere else in the Old Testament and belongs to later Hebrew. Delitzsch takes the two-example reading, following Jerome and Luther, and explains the second clause as a shortened comparison, meaning the reader's ignorance about the growth of the bones. Gill records both possibilities without choosing, and Wesley keeps to the soul, how it comes into the child and how it is united with the body. Clarke applies the ignorance where he has applied everything else: a man cannot tell why God allowed these particular people to fall into want, and should take care that what he calls scrupulousness is not really the love of money.

On sowing morning and evening the readings converge. Delitzsch takes tillage as the prototype of all work and this sowing as an emblem of activity in any calling, and insists the point is not that labour never stops but that it continues until evening. Wesley says the same in his own idiom, early and late and in all seasons, speedily and continually. Gill gives the two mornings, of youth and of prosperity. Clarke returns once more to charity, and states the principle that governs his whole reading: since a giver cannot know which object is worthiest, God will reward him not by the merit of the person relieved but by the motive that moved him to relieve.
7:
That the light is sweet nobody disputes, and Delitzsch spends his note on precision. He objects to two translators who render the connecting particle truly or yes, which gives the clause a false colouring, and to a scholar who made light stand for life: the word means the light of life in this world, of which the sun is the source. He then quotes Euripides, including a plea that a girl's youth not be destroyed, since to see the light is sweet. Henry allows the sweetness at length and turns it into an argument: light was the first thing made in the great world as the eye is among the first in the little one, the heathen were so charmed by it that they worshipped the sun, and life is sweet to bad men because their portion is in it, to good men because it is their time of preparation, to all men because nature says so — whence he warns that we must double our guard lest we love it too well. Gill runs the word through natural light, prosperity and life, and records an older reading making it the light of the law.

The days of darkness are handled soberly. Clarke observes that a man who does not die violently will die lingeringly, ordinarily with many pains, and adds a saying from Ecclesiasticus, that whoever remembers his end in all he undertakes will never do amiss. Wesley reads the darkness as death or the state of the dead, those days far outnumbering the days of this short life. Henry keeps the verse's balance: we should think of death in the midst of life, precisely when it is sweetest.

The charge to the young man is the chapter's hardest thing, and they divide over its tone. Gill takes it as plain advice, of temporal enjoyment within lawful limits or of spiritual gladness, since young men who remember their Creator should rejoice in him. Clarke begins in the same key, that a gracious God has ordered the young to be free of cares and to rejoice, then turns the verse on the reader: if you will follow the propensities of your own heart, the noisy mirth of the fool and the dissipation of the profligate, go on, take your full swing — but take this with you, that for all these things God will judge you. Wesley reads it so too, telling the young man to deny his eye nothing and then consider his reckoning. Ellicott moves the question elsewhere. He thinks the chapter division would sit better here, and argues that the judgment named can hardly mean anything but a future one, given how much of the book complains that retribution does not happen in this life. Delitzsch confines himself to grammar: the preposition marks the joy's proper time, not its ground.

The final verse turns on one noun, and the renderings split three ways. Delitzsch reports that Jerome translated it anger and understood by that every disturbance of the mind, and objects that the Hebrew covers sadness, moroseness and fretfulness together; he objects again on the parallel clause, Jerome having taken the evil removed from the flesh as bodily indulgence where the sense is physical — one word names what brings sorrow to the heart, the other what harms the body. Clarke and Gill keep anger and widen it to every violent passion, Gill adding the older suggestion that what is meant is whatever provokes God. Wesley takes the opposite road and reads sensual lusts, which the writer elegantly calls sorrow because they gratify the senses now and bring intolerable sorrow soon. Ellicott adds that the word for youth occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament though a near relative describes black hair; Clarke ends where the chapter is going: childhood and youth come to nothing, eternity alone is permanent, and a man should live for it.
